paras: The Centreville roadside ambush was a shooting near Centreville, Texas, in February 1882, in which a white man named Lyle fired from hiding on two Black men named Hall and their wives as they rode in a wagon. Both men were killed and both women were reported mortally wounded. Carried by a St. Louis telegraph dispatch, the story ran in papers from West Virginia to California under headlines such as "Negroes Waylaid and Shot" and "Double Murder."

According to the dispatch, the two men, riding along the road in a wagon, "had some trouble with the child of a white man named Lyle." The child ran home and told its father. The Canton Register described the episode as "a feud growing out of a trivial circumstance" and said the men had "some words" with the child.

Lyle took a shotgun and hid by the roadside, or in the Canton Register's words "lay in ambush along the roadside." When the two men and their wives drove past, he fired on the wagon, "almost blowing the heads off the men and fatally wounding the women." The dispatch, dated St. Louis, February 19, said the shooting happened "yesterday," that is, February 18, and the Canton Register likewise placed it "last Saturday."
Lyle fled, and officers started in pursuit. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage, and no later report says whether the two women died.

The story reached readers almost entirely through a single St. Louis telegram, printed nearly word for word on February 20 by the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Wheeling Register. Over the following week it was reprinted or cut down in Nevada, Iowa, Oregon, Wisconsin, Illinois and Montana, often in columns of condensed telegraph news. Editors headed it "A DEADLY SHOT," "Terrible Tragedy," "A DOUBLE MURDER" and "A Quadruple Tragedy," and the wire text itself called Lyle "the murderer."

The reports named the victims only by surname, called them "negroes," and did not discuss race as a motive. The St. Paul Globe's headline, "Negroes Waylaid and Shot," put the victims first, while the Canton Register framed the killings as the outgrowth of a petty quarrel.

Condensed versions gave other dates: the Los Angeles Herald re-dated the dispatch February 20 while keeping "yesterday," the Dillon Tribune said "on Sunday," and one news summary said "on the 20th." The earliest full dispatch and the Canton Register agree on February 18, and the later variants appear to come from re-dating as the story was condensed.

reader.title: Centreville roadside ambush
bases: The dispatch describes one white man, Lyle, shooting two Black men and their wives from ambush after a quarrel with his child, with no mob, band or posse involved (A1, A2, A6).

Every version traces to one St. Louis telegraphic dispatch reprinted or condensed across the country (A1, A2, A3, A6); no local Texas report or independent account appears in the coverage, and none contradicts it.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire dispatch
accounts.gist: After the men had trouble with Lyle's child, who ran home and told him, Lyle hid by the road with a shotgun and fired on the wagon, nearly blowing the men's heads off and fatally wounding the women; he fled with officers in pursuit.

accounts.label: Condensed rewrite (Canton Register)
accounts.gist: Calls it a feud from a trivial circumstance: after words with his child, Lyle lay in ambush and fired on the two men and their wives in a wagon, killing the men and mortally wounding the women.

framing.detail: Papers from Minnesota to California ran the St. Louis dispatch nearly word for word under headlines such as 'Negroes Waylaid and Shot', 'A DEADLY SHOT' and 'Terrible Texas', calling Lyle 'the murderer'.
The Canton Register's rewrite cast the killings as 'a feud growing out of a trivial circumstance' that 'developed into a fearful tragedy'.

versions.value: 'Yesterday' in a St. Louis dispatch dated Feb. 19 (Feb. 18)

conflicts.note: The earliest full dispatch, dated Feb. 19 and printed Feb. 20, puts the shooting on Feb. 18, which fell on a Saturday in 1882 and so matches the Canton Register; the later variants look like re-dating as the story was condensed.
'Hail' appears only in raw OCR of the Dillon Tribune (and OCR of one reprint); a clean re-read of the same Dillon text, and every other version, prints 'Hall'.
